edges.effect_quant: Across older probiotic meta-analyses, the signal is modest: fewer upper-respiratory infections and shorter illness episodes rather than a dramatic elimination of risk.
edges.population: otherwise healthy children and adults using oral probiotic supplements
edges.mechanism: Probiotics may influence mucosal immunity and antiviral defense through gut-immune signaling, but the effect depends heavily on strain, dose, and baseline host context. That strain-dependence is exactly why the clinical signal is real but not huge.
edges.summary: The best synthesis is still the Cochrane review, which found fewer people developing acute upper respiratory infections and shorter illness duration with probiotics than with placebo. Later meta-analyses broadly agree, but they also remind us that the benefit is modest and not every strain performs the same way.
edges.caveats: This edge collapses many probiotic strains into one label, which hides meaningful heterogeneity. It should be read as a low-to-moderate confidence class effect rather than a guarantee that any probiotic product will help.

evidence.citation: Hao Q et al 2015 Cochrane Database Syst Rev
evidence.notes: Probiotics for preventing acute upper respiratory tract infections.

effect_quant.comparator: at least one acute upper respiratory infection with probiotics versus placebo

evidence.citation: King S et al 2014 Br J Nutr
evidence.notes: Effectiveness of probiotics on the duration of illness in healthy children and adults who develop common acute respiratory infectious conditions: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: duration of acute respiratory illness with probiotics versus placebo
